PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
CON
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
CON
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
CON
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

### Background
#### Reserves
***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal.
During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
***Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.*** Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits.
The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).

### Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting.
It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies.
Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030).
In addition, Prop.
2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit,” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong.
The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20.

Proposition 2 would allow California to build a larger financial cushion

## Analysis of Measure
### Background
#### Reserves
***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal.
During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
***Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.*** Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits.
The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
#### Debt

### Additional Titles
Rainy day Fund

### Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting.
It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies.
Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030).
In addition, Prop.
2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit,” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong.
The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20.

**SUPPORT POSITION: Proposition 2 — “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”**
On August 8, 2026, the California State PTA Board of Managers voted to approve a SUPPORT position on Proposition 2.
**What This Measure Proposes:** Proposition 2 raises the Budget Stabilization Account (rainy day fund) deposit cap from 10% to 20% of general fund revenue, exempts those deposits from the state spending limit (the Gann Limit), and extends the state’s required extra debt payments through 2040.
**Why We Took This Position:** A larger, more resilient rainy day fund gives the state greater capacity to protect school funding when the economy and stock market turn down, consistent with PTA’s legislative platform commitment to fiscal responsibility in government and to safeguarding public schools’ constitutional first claim on general fund revenue.

### Background

***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.

- Historical precedent: The 2014 Prop 2 (rainy day fund rules) passed 68.9%-31.1%. Legislative constitutional amendments on budget/reserves tend to pass.

The question: "Which side is more likely to win?" Answer with only "yes" or "no." So the YES side is more likely to win. Answer: "yes."

Let me consider whether the election may have already occurred — the IGS page lists "Certified Results" with blank values. The cityhallpass page was "Updated November 2, 2026" saying "First results appear here after that" — suggesting results aren't out yet, or we're right before/around election day. Either way, all evidence points to YES being far ahead (60-61% in polls, bipartisan, no organized opposition).

The answer: yes.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.

PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
CON
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

### Background
#### Reserves
***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal.
During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
***Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.*** Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits.
The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).

## Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
### Additional Titles
Rainy day Fund
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
### Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting.
It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies.
Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030).
In addition, Prop.
2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit,” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong.
The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20.

Proposition 2 would allow California to build a larger financial cushion

Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs).
